explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), says it plainly: “…a mocker does not listen to rebuke.” The mocker is the one who does not listen. Set beside him is the wise son who heeds his father's discipline.
Solomon never brings up a servant in this verse. The one who does not listen to rebuke is a mocker. He's set right next to the wise son who heeds his father's discipline.

No stranger walks into this verse, friend. Solomon, David's son and Israel's king (Proverbs 1:1), names the mocker as the one who does not listen to rebuke. The other side of the matchup is the wise son, who heeds his father's discipline.

Close, but the verse lands somewhere else. It says the desire of the faithless is violence, not peace. The first half goes the other way: from the fruit of his lips a man enjoys good things. Two very different appetites.

Right, baker. The verse says the desire of the faithless is violence, and peace isn't in it. Across from that, a man enjoys good things from the fruit of his lips. Solomon sets the two statements side by side.

Yes, guarding his mouth. “He who guards his mouth protects his life, but the one who opens his lips invites his own ruin.” Solomon sets two men side by side. One guards his mouth and protects his life, and the other opens his lips and invites his own ruin. Keep that mouth on a short leash, friend.

Gold is a fair guess, but this verse never mentions it. Solomon says the one who guards his mouth protects his life. Riches do come up a few verses later, in verse 8, where they may ransom a man's life, but that's a different matchup.
Good locks are nice, friend, but Solomon isn't talking about doors. He says the man who guards his mouth protects his life. The man who opens his lips invites his own ruin.
That's the one. The slacker craves yet has nothing, but the soul of the diligent is “fully satisfied.” The diligent person doesn't just get by, he gets full. That's a good place to end up.
Restless is a fair guess, but it isn't the word in this verse. Solomon says the slacker craves yet has nothing, and the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied. The diligent end up satisfied.
Nobody gets ignored in this verse. Solomon is talking about what each person ends up with. The slacker craves yet has nothing, and the soul of the diligent is fully satisfied.

Yes. “Righteousness guards the man of integrity, but wickedness undermines the sinner.” Righteousness does the guarding, and wickedness does the undermining. So the one who gets guarded is the man of integrity. Picture a cookie box with the bottom already gone.
Protection is the job of righteousness in this verse. It guards the man of integrity. Wickedness does the opposite, because it undermines the sinner.
No promotion for the sinner here, friend. Solomon says wickedness undermines him. The one who gets guarded is the man of integrity, and righteousness does the guarding.

True, baker. One pretends to be rich but has nothing, and another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. Solomon is pointing out that what you see on the outside doesn't always match what's in the pockets. Looks can be fooling.
Solomon really does say it. Verse 7 gives two opposite pretenders. One pretends to be rich but has nothing, and another pretends to be poor, yet has great wealth. So this one is true.
Yes. Riches may ransom a man's life, but a poor man hears no threat. Solomon doesn't say which life is easier, he just lays the two side by side. Let him make the point, friend.
I'd love a little applause too, but this verse isn't handing any out. Solomon says riches may ransom a man's life, but a poor man hears no threat. That's the word you're after, baker.
No band is playing in this verse, friend. Solomon says a poor man hears no threat. That sits beside the line about riches ransoming a man's life.
Not quite. Verse 9 says the light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished. That lamp goes out. It doesn't keep burning.
Right, baker. The light of the righteous shines brightly, but the lamp of the wicked is extinguished. It goes out. Solomon sets a bright light next to a dark one.

Yes, advice. “Arrogance leads only to strife, but wisdom is with the well-advised.” Solomon says wisdom is with the well-advised, the people who take advice. Arrogance, on the other hand, leads only to strife. So wisdom shows up where advice is welcome.
Taking the credit feels good, but it isn't what Solomon is saying. He says arrogance leads only to strife, and wisdom is with the well-advised. The well-advised are the people who take advice.
Shortcuts are tempting, friend, but they're not in this verse. Solomon says wisdom is with the well-advised. Arrogance, on the other hand, leads only to strife.

That's it. “Dishonest wealth will dwindle, but what is earned through hard work will be multiplied.” Dishonest wealth is the one that dwindles. What is earned through hard work is the part that gets multiplied. So one kind of wealth shrinks and the other grows.
Solomon says the opposite about dishonest wealth. It will dwindle. It's the wealth earned through hard work that gets multiplied.
Double is a fair guess, but Solomon uses a different word. He says what is earned through hard work will be multiplied. Dishonest wealth goes the other direction and dwindles.

True. Verse 12 says, “Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but desire fulfilled is a tree of life.” Solomon names both the sick heart and the tree of life. The second half is the one this card asked about.
Solomon does say it. After the sick heart from hope deferred, he says desire fulfilled is a tree of life. So this one is true, friend.

True, baker. Solomon says the one who despises instruction will pay the penalty, but the one who respects a command will be rewarded. Following the instructions has a payoff. Fewer leftover screws, I'd say.
Solomon actually says this. In verse 13, the one who despises instruction will pay the penalty. But the one who respects a command will be rewarded. So it's true.
Yes. The teaching of the wise is “…a fountain of life, turning one from the snares of death.” A snare is a trap. The teaching turns a person away from it.
The house of mourning doesn't appear in this verse. Solomon says the teaching of the wise turns one from the snares of death. That's the danger it steers around.
No ocean in this verse, friend. Solomon says the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life. It turns one from the snares of death.
Not quite. Solomon says the prudent man acts with knowledge, but a fool displays his folly. He puts it out for everyone to see. It's not hidden at all.
Right. A fool doesn't keep his folly hidden, he displays it. Every prudent man acts with knowledge, but the fool shows his folly right out in the open. No apron big enough to cover that.
Yes. A wicked messenger falls into trouble, but a faithful envoy brings healing. Solomon puts the two messengers side by side. The faithful one brings healing, and that's a good job to have.
Late messengers are a pain, I'll grant you, but delay isn't in this verse. Solomon says a faithful envoy brings healing. The wicked messenger is the one who falls into trouble.
Confusion is not what the faithful envoy brings, friend. Solomon says he brings healing. The wicked messenger falls into trouble.
That's the one. Poverty and shame come to him who ignores discipline, but whoever heeds correction is honored. Taking correction ends in honor. That's a good trade for a little humility.
Shame is real in this verse, but it lands on the other side. Poverty and shame come to him who ignores discipline. Whoever heeds correction is honored.
Nobody is forgotten in this verse, baker. Solomon says whoever heeds correction is honored. Poverty and shame belong to the one who ignores discipline.
Yes. Desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul, but turning from evil is detestable to fools. That's a hard thing to read. Fools don't want to turn from it.
Waiting their turn isn't in this verse. Solomon says turning from evil is detestable to fools. The other half is that desire fulfilled is sweet to the soul.
No field work in this verse, friend. What's detestable to fools is turning from evil. Desire fulfilled, meanwhile, is sweet to the soul.
Yes. He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed. Who you walk with matters. It's worth picking your walking buddies carefully.
Solomon doesn't promise riches here. He says the companion of fools will be destroyed. It's the one who walks with the wise who becomes wise.
Nobody's envying him in this verse, friend. Solomon says the companion of fools will be destroyed. The one who walks with the wise becomes wise.
True, baker. Disaster pursues sinners, but prosperity is the reward of the righteous. Solomon sets the two paths side by side. Disaster chases one, and the other gets a reward.
Solomon does say this. In verse 21, disaster pursues sinners, but prosperity is the reward of the righteous. So the statement is true.

Yes, righteous. “A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children, but the sinner’s wealth is passed to the righteous.” The sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous, and that's the whole answer. The good man, meanwhile, leaves an inheritance to his children's children. Not the owner's plan, I bet.
Neighbors aren't named here. Solomon says the sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous. The good man, meanwhile, leaves an inheritance to his children's children.
No priests in this verse, friend. The sinner's wealth is passed to the righteous. A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children.

Yes. “Abundant food is in the fallow ground of the poor, but without justice it is swept away.” The food was there, and it still got swept away. Solomon names the cause plainly: without justice. So the lack of justice is what takes the abundance.
Rain isn't in this verse. Solomon says the abundant food in the fallow ground of the poor is swept away without justice. That's the cause the text gives.
No locusts here, friend. The food in the fallow ground of the poor is swept away without justice. That's what Solomon says.

That's the one. He who spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him diligently. Solomon links love with the diligence of discipline. It's a heavy one to read, and he says it plain.
Excusing is the opposite of what the verse says. The father who loves his son disciplines him diligently. The one who spares the rod hates his son.
Spoiling isn't in this verse, baker. Solomon says the father who loves his son disciplines him diligently. Sparing the rod, on the other side, is called hating him.
Not quite. Solomon says a righteous man eats to his heart's content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty. Empty, not full. That's the part this card flipped.

Right, that one is false. Solomon says, “A righteous man eats to his heart’s content, but the stomach of the wicked is empty.” The stomach of the wicked is empty, not full. The righteous man is the one who eats to his heart's content.
